Yesterday saw two conflicting reports about next year's 20th-anniversary iPhone model, which is said to embody Apple's long-term vision of "a single sheet of glass."

Reports on what we can actually expect have already been at odds, but yesterday's divergence was the most stark to date…

The current situation

Former Apple design chief Jony Ive has frequently spoken of his long-term vision of the iPhone eventually becoming a single sheet of glass. It is widely believed that Apple has retained this vision after Ive's departure.

Although Apple generally does not make a big deal of celebrating various anniversaries of its products, the consensus view is that they are aiming to get as close as possible to this vision by the iPhone's 20th anniversary. This is likely to include embedding Face ID technology beneath the display, as well as hiding the front-facing camera under the screen as well.

However, we have already seen conflicting reports on expectations. While the original view was that this would be a standalone model similar to the iPhone Air and the upcoming iPhone Ultra, more recent reports have suggested that the design will instead be used on next year's iPhone Pro models.

Counting in order, this would be the iPhone 19 Pro, but Apple may also want to mark the anniversary by skipping this generation and going straight to the iPhone 20 name.

Yesterday's conflicting reports

Things got even more confused yesterday when an analyst suggested Apple had abandoned the idea of an all-glass iPhone next year.

However, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman quickly shot down this claim.

The more likely reality

The point is that Apple's vision for the iPhone does not have a single final destination. Whatever they plan to release next year will only be one or a few steps toward the sci-fi vision of "a single sheet of glass."

The question is not whether that goal will be reached next year, but how far Apple will move toward this vision. But whether it is one step or several, it certainly will not be the final step in the evolution of the iPhone's design.

In fact, Gurman revealed that Apple has stepped back from the extent they had originally hoped to achieve by next year.

Jefferies analysts likely heard the same news, but only more recently, and therefore mistakenly believed the plan had been completely abandoned.

My own expectation is that next year's design will be a major step forward—on par with the breakthrough of the iPhone X launch—but there will be further developments in the years to come. For me, the biggest question is whether the 2027 iPhone will feature enough of a leap to warrant Apple adopting some kind of special branding, such as being labelled a 20th-anniversary iPhone (which I think is extremely unlikely), being given some other special name, or skipping a generation to be called the iPhone 20.

What are your expectations? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
